title: Stack: operating systems that invented everything first
subtitle: 11 cards on top of the archive: Plan 9 and Inferno, BeOS and BFS, Cairo→WinFS, Newton Soup, Workplace OS, TRON and μITRON, FM Towns, Self — plus a build card “an OS for a local agent” from ten decisions.
about: A stack about the system layer: namespaces and 9P, an image instead of a restart, a live query instead of a folder, a structural store, microkernel “personalities”. Every card rests on a verified archive entry.
archive_title: Ideas that didn't survive: Japanese and world software, 1980–2006 (RU)

home.title: Operating systems that invented everything first — and were left without a market
home.subtitle: stack home · 11 cards · archive 1984–2006

fields.val: Almost everything now called the modern system layer was built and tested in the 1980s–2000s: per-process namespaces, mounting instead of APIs, live queries, structural stores, microkernel “personalities”, an image instead of a restart. The problem with those systems was never the ideas — it was the market. This stack exists so you take the ready solutions instead of reinventing them one at a time.

Cards on the left, ← → pages through them. Every card carries an “⌗ archive entry” link (a verified finding with sources) and a “links” block; the reverse side of every link is visible too, under “links here”.
Not a history textbook and not a rating. Facts (years, numbers, names) come from archive entries; the “what to build” blocks and the “gap” score are the agent's judgement, marked as judgement.

plan9.title: Plan 9 — “mount, don't integrate”
plan9.subtitle: 1992/1995 — present · Bell Labs · 9P, namespaces, union directories

fields.val: A Bell Labs operating system (1992 for universities, 1995 public, fourth edition in 2021): every process has its own name space, union directories, “everything is a file”, the 9P network protocol, and the rio window system.
Unix rewritten from scratch: mounting instead of APIs, one protocol for any resource, network resources that look like local files rather than “SDK clients”.
Dogmatic adherence to the model, no Unix compatibility, and competition from a free Linux.
The technology won incognito: Linux namespaces, union/overlay mounts, WSL1, virtio-9p in QEMU — all Plan 9 ideas, often without credit.

9P as a minimal universal protocol for accessing resources (files, devices, telemetry) instead of dozens of REST APIs. “Mount, don't integrate” dramatically simplifies service and agent wiring: a new source is a mount point, not a new client.

links.inferno: the same 9P, but with bytecode and migration
links.build: the first build decision: a name space as the interface
links.winfs: a different answer to “where does structure live”

inferno.title: Inferno — bytecode as the unit of deployment
inferno.subtitle: 1995 — present · Bell Labs / Vita Nuova · Dis, Limbo, Styx

fields.val: A Bell Labs operating system (1995, now MIT-licensed): the kernel is the Dis virtual machine, the language is Limbo, the network protocol is Styx (9P), the interface is Tk. The motto was “one OS on any device”.
A commercial failure (Vita Nuova); it lost to Java/JVM on ecosystem and tooling.
The ideas fully coincided with what WASM does: a portable bytecode, one artefact for every device, boundaries between machines dissolved.
“Bytecode plus a mounted name space” is a complete architecture for a local-first application with honest migration between devices. Today it is assembled from two halves: WASM and 9P.

links.plan9: the heir of 9P and of the namespace model
links.self: another answer to “what state is saved”: an image versus bytecode
links.build: the second build decision: the deployment artefact

beos.title: BeOS and BFS — a live query instead of a folder
beos.subtitle: 1995 — 2001 · Be Inc. · BFS: attributes, journalling, live queries

fields.val: Be Inc.'s operating system (first release 1995, last R5.0.3 in 2000; Palm bought the assets in 2001): C++, aggressive multithreading, media-first. BFS brought a 64-bit address space, journalling, extended attributes and live queries.
Responsiveness as an architectural property: priorities and streaming optimisations in the file system, attribute metadata, and live queries — a folder as a saved query that updates itself.
Not enough market share and not enough money: sales were poor, the platform lost to Windows and Apple, the assets were sold off.
Dead as an OS, but Haiku keeps development going; live queries and attributes have been partly reinvented in Spotlight, SQLite and Datomic.

A live query as a first-class interface object (a board that updates itself) plus extended attributes as a system metadata layer over local files: a local data graph instead of “folders as junk drawers”.

links.winfs: both cards are about metadata and schema; BeOS did it in the file system, Microsoft in a database under the OS
links.newton: records with indices as an alternative to files
links.build: the third build decision: live views

actions.t: Compare with Spotlight and Datomic
actions.p: Compare the BFS approach (attributes + live queries) with Spotlight, SQLite FTS and Datomic: what of the live model is actually available to a developer today. Facts with links.

winfs.title: Cairo → WinFS — a file system as a knowledge base
winfs.subtitle: 1991 — 2006 · Microsoft · cancelled 23 June 2006

fields.val: Microsoft's line from “Cairo” (1991) to WinFS: an OS on top of a native database — an object file system, schemas, relationships between documents, search by metadata.
Announced in the WinFS team blog on 23 June 2006: complexity, performance requirements, and no applications ready to consume the schema. Part of the technology went into SQL Server and ADO.NET.
Partly: Spotlight, tags, Datomic. As a system-level schema layer WinFS does not exist — the idea returned as “local databases inside applications”.

A local graph with types and migrations: SQLite/DuckDB underneath, a schema and indices as a system service. This is exactly what makes personal agents reliable — data gets structure instead of being flat text.

links.newton: the same bet: records with a schema instead of files
links.beos: metadata at the file-system level — the working alternative
links.build: the fourth build decision: a schema with migrations

actions.p: Design a minimal local graph schema for personal documents: object types, relationships, version migrations, indices for live queries. SQLite/DuckDB, no cloud. Start from cards winfs and newton.

actions.p: Establish from primary sources the reasons WinFS was cancelled (the team blog, the 2006 press): what exactly failed — performance, missing applications, complexity. Give quotes and links.

newton.title: Newton “Soup” — a structural store at the OS level
newton.subtitle: 1993 — 1998 · Apple · object store and soups

fields.val: The Apple Newton storage layer: all memory was an object store plus “soups” — simple single-table databases of records with indices and queries; one object data model for every application.
Data as structure, not files: applications exchanged records, and search, synchronisation and cross-application transfer worked out of the box.
The PDA line was closed in 1998; on bigger machines the “files and folders” model won over records with indices.
Dead; its closest relatives are Core Data, SQLite inside applications, and local databases.

A single structural store at the OS level: one record store with indices, relationships and soups instead of scattered files and schemas. This is the foundation of local-first applications and agents: an agent reads structure instead of re-parsing documents.

links.winfs: the same idea, but through a schema and a database under the OS
links.build: the fifth build decision: a record store

actions.t: Compare Soup with Core Data and SQLite
actions.p: Compare Newton Soup with Core Data and raw SQLite: what the object storage model gives you, what is lost, what it costs. Give a table and a conclusion on what to take for a local agent.

actions.t: Build a soup prototype in 20 lines
actions.p: Build a minimal “soup” prototype in Python/SQLite: a record table, indices, a pattern query, and a change subscription. Show working code and its output.

wpos.title: IBM Workplace OS — “personalities” on a microkernel
wpos.subtitle: 1991 — 1996 · Mach 3.0 · OS/2 + Unix + DOS + AIX on one machine

fields.val: An IBM project on the Mach 3.0 microkernel: “personalities” that let one machine run unmodified OS/2, Unix, DOS and AIX applications. The final PowerPC preview came in January 1996.
Performance and cost: the microkernel plus personalities added overhead. IBM never brought it to market — RTM in December 1995, an attempt in January 1996, then cancellation.
The idea won in a new guise: containers, WSL, virtual machines, gVisor. “Personalities” became routine — just under other names.

“API compatibility as a service”: not emulating everything, but precise behavioural contracts plus compatibility tests. This is a market for legacy migration for decades to come — and an honest alternative to “rewrite everything”.

links.tron: TRON solved the same problem differently: one contract instead of a set of personalities
links.build: the sixth build decision: compatibility as a contract

actions.t: Compare WPoS with WSL and containers
actions.p: Compare Workplace OS “personalities” with WSL2, gVisor and containers: where the compatibility boundary sits, what the overhead costs, and what counts as a sufficient contract. Links to documentation.

actions.t: Estimate a migration of my legacy
actions.p: Estimate migrating my project from <platform> to <platform> as a “personality”: what must be preserved, which behavioural contracts need tests, and where emulation is cheaper than a rewrite.

tron.title: TRON — one contract from a microwave to a workstation
tron.subtitle: 1984 — present · Ken Sakamura · ITRON / BTRON / MTRON / STRON

fields.val: An open real-time OS architecture: ITRON (embedded), BTRON (personal systems), MTRON/STRON — plus a free licence on the specifications. Led by Ken Sakamura of the University of Tokyo.

“Computers everywhere” seven years before Weiser's paper: one contract from a microwave oven to a workstation; open specifications and a free licence long before open source became mainstream. An IEEE Milestone.

Incompatibility with the DOS world: NEC held 80–90% of Japan's education market on DOS, so switching meant throwing away the whole infrastructure and software stack. BTRON286 prototypes were tested in schools in 1988, but mass adoption never happened.
The ITRON branch won invisibly — billions of devices. BTRON is history; the project lives on as the TRON Forum plus T-Kernel/T-Engine.

An end-to-end architecture at the component level: one contract (today that is the WASM Component Model + WASI) over an RTOS, so device and cloud code are assembled from the same interfaces. Plus the compatibility lesson: an architecture that demands throwing away what exists is never adopted.

links.towns: a Japanese machine killed by incompatibility with the PC world
links.build: the seventh build decision: one contract at every level

itron.title: μITRON / T-Kernel — the invisible winner
itron.subtitle: 1984 — present · an RTOS specification · billions of devices

fields.val: A specification of an RTOS kernel for microcomputers: ITRON first (1984), then μITRON and T-Kernel/T-Engine (2001+). A specification, not code.
Dozens of vendors implemented it independently — hence its presence in billions of devices, from washing machines and cameras to automotive units. An open standard before the open-source fashion.
As a product it was never a brand: training and community stayed in Japan, while FreeRTOS, Zephyr and VxWorks won worldwide.
Alive (T-Kernel, TOPPERS); relevant as a base for edge AI on microcontrollers.

An open RTOS specification as “POSIX for hardware” plus a WASM sandbox for updatable models on the device: portability across MCUs and updates without vendor lock-in. A specification rather than a brand is the cheapest way to win invisibly.

links.tron: the parent project: the same philosophy of “a spec, not code”
links.build: the eighth build decision: a specification as the product

actions.p: Compare μITRON/T-Kernel with Zephyr and FreeRTOS: the API model, licences, portability, and the presence of a WASM sandbox. Give a table and a conclusion on what to take for edge AI.

towns.title: FM Towns and X68000 — a creator-first OS
towns.subtitle: 1987 — 1990s · Towns OS, Human68k, SX-Window

fields.val: Japanese “multimedia” personal systems of the late 1980s: Fujitsu FM Towns (Towns OS, CD-ROM, 32,768 colours) and Sharp X68000 (Human68k plus the SX-Window GUI, sound and graphics at arcade-machine level).
Ready-made workstations for creators: colour, sound, CD-ROM as standard and a windowed interface — earlier than Windows 3.1 and clearly better than the “home” PCs of the time.
Proprietary, expensive, and isolated inside Japan; PC clones with DOS/V and game consoles finished them off.
Dead, except for emulators, collectors and the retro demoscene.

A creator-first OS: guaranteed I/O latency, colour calibration, an audio/MIDI graph and deterministic timing as system guarantees rather than as a pile of workarounds in pro audio and video. Today applications do this; it should be a property of the platform.

links.beos: a media-first OS: the same bet on responsiveness and timing
links.build: the ninth build decision: timing as a guarantee

actions.p: Define what “deterministic timing as a platform guarantee” means: which metrics (input latency, audio jitter, frame pacing), how to measure them, and where they break on a normal OS.

actions.t: Find living analogues
actions.p: Find who provides creator-first guarantees at the OS/platform level today (Audio Workgroups, CoreAudio, PipeWire, realtime kernels): what exactly is guaranteed, with documentation links.

self.title: Self and Smalltalk — an image instead of a restart
self.subtitle: 1972 / 1987 — present · prototypes, adaptive optimisation, the live image

fields.val: Self (Ungar, Smith, 1987): objects without classes, prototypes and “morphing”; adaptive optimisation — inline caching, polymorphic inline caches, type feedback — was invented there. Smalltalk (1972): the system lives as an image of objects and is edited while running.
Self the language did not survive (it evolved into the Klein VM) and Smalltalk was displaced by the mainstream; the “image as a deployment artefact” model lost to files and git.
The technique won silently: Self's JIT optimisations are inside every JS and JVM engine — V8, HotSpot. Live environments survive in Squeak/Pharo, notebooks and front-end live reload.

Bring the “image” back in a new shape: saved session state and durable execution for local applications and agents, editable while running, instead of “restart from scratch”. Plus interfaces that morph themselves to the task rather than static forms.

links.inferno: another road to portable state: bytecode and an OS virtual machine
links.build: the tenth build decision: an image and durable execution

actions.p: Design a “session image” for a local agent: what is saved, how it is restored after a crash, how it is edited while running. Compare with durable execution (workflow engines) and notebooks.

actions.p: Verify from sources which Self techniques (inline caching, PIC, type feedback) are actually used in V8 and HotSpot today, and when they arrived. Links are mandatory.

build.title: Build: an OS for a local agent from ten decisions
build.subtitle: the stack's practical output · 10 decisions from 10 cards

fields.val: A new data source is a mount point (9P/facade), not a new SDK. The consumer sees files and directories.

fields.lbl: Bytecode as the unit of deployment
fields.val: One artefact (WASM) for device, server and browser; boundaries between machines are mounting, not rewriting.
A board or folder is a saved query that updates itself. No “rebuild the list by hand”.

fields.lbl: A record store, not a file store
fields.val: One structural store with indices: an agent reads structure instead of re-parsing documents.
Types and relationships as a system service (SQLite/DuckDB plus schema). Without it a “structural store” becomes a JSON dump.
Legacy migration means precise behavioural contracts and tests, not emulating the whole world.
A component model (WASM Component Model + WASI) from microcontroller to cloud — otherwise two stacks forever.
An open spec that others implement wins invisibly and outlives any vendor.
Input latency, audio jitter and frame pacing are platform properties, not workarounds in an application.
Session state is saved and edited while running; a crash does not mean lost work.

links.newton: without a structural store nothing else works
